chunks: "A servo motor is a motor packaged with a sensor and a controller so that it goes to a commanded position and holds it.
The motor itself can be an ordinary brushed DC motor or a brushless one.

What makes it a servo is the feedback loop: a sensor on the output shaft tells a controller where the shaft actually is, the controller compares that to where I asked it to be, and it drives the motor in whichever direction shrinks the error.
The hobby version is what most people have seen.
It's a small DC motor, a gearbox, a potentiometer on the output shaft, and a little control board, all in a plastic case with three wires: power, ground and a signal.
I send it a pulse every 20 milliseconds, and the pulse width, typically 1 to 2 milliseconds, says which angle I want.
The industrial version is the same idea with a brushless motor, an encoder with thousands of counts per turn, and a separate drive that runs nested current, speed and position loops.
So in one line: a servo is a motor plus feedback, and the feedback is what gives you accuracy, holding torque and the ability to reject disturbances."
